newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Chrysler sees worldwide sales up in 1997.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Chrysler sees worldwide sales up in 1997.

text.p: Chrysler Corp chief executive officer Robert Eaton said on Tuesday Chrysler saw its U.S. sales down slightly in calendar 1997 from 1996, but that overall sales worldwide should be higher for the year.
"Clearly the U.S. is going to be down a little bit from 1996. Europe is going to about the same, or maybe a little bit higher," Eaton told a media luncheon in Sydney.
"I would hope we will exceed last year," he said, when asked what Chrysler expected for the full year.
Eaton said Chrysler sold 2.967 million vehicles in 1996, creating pre-tax profits of US$6 billion.

He said Chrysler had the strongest balance sheet of any automaker outside of Toyota Motor Co and had returned US$3 billion of capital in 1996 to shareholders, including a US$1 billion dividend and US$2 billion of stock buy-backs.
"We are doing the same thing this year," he said. "We're well on the way to the US$2 billion buyback this year."
Eaton said Chrysler expected to rapidly increase the international component of its total sales.
Chrysler's total sales were US$61 billion in 1996 and included US$5 billion outside the United States, he said.
"We expect that US$5 billion outside the U.S. to double over the next three years and double again by the end of the next decade," he said.
Eaton said Chrysler expected to continue to be an importer of niche vehicles in Australia for the foreseeable future, as it did not have large enough volumes to sustain local production.
He added that in general he favoured the continual lowering of trade barriers and opening of markets.
The Australian car industry and the government are currently debating an official report recommending a faster rate of tariff reduction on imported cars.
Currently the tariffs are scheduled to be cut to 15 percent by 2000 from 25 percent currently, but the report said they should be cut to five percent by 2004.
Eaton later said the yen's recent devaluation was the biggest factor affecting the U.S. market.
"I think the big issue out there is the yen," Eaton said.
Eaton, who is on the U.S. President's Advisory Committe on Trade Policy and Negotiation, later told reporters it was dramatically undervalued and the Japanese government had manipulated it lower.
"We believe quite frankly that the structural rate of the yen should be somewhere around 100 (yen to the dollar)," he said.
"All we want is the Japanese government to do is to stay the hell out of the market," he said.
"In the yen, they're the ones who have been distorting the market. It hasn't anything to do with being a rational, free and open market," he said.
At 0450 GMT the U.S. dollar was trading at 123.44/49 yen.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
